# 4. The Queue Abstraction

The queue is the most important abstraction in the system. The application code calls the same interface regardless of environment — what's underneath changes.

### Queue Implementation Per Environment

| Environment | Queue Backend | Worker |
|-------------|---------------|--------|
| Development | MongoDB jobs | Local worker (poll-based) |
| Vercel | MongoDB jobs | Vercel Cron / serverless |
| Azure | Azure Service Bus | Container Apps |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Dev[Development]
        D1[enqueueJob] --> D2[MongoDB Jobs] --> D3[Local Worker]
    end
    subgraph Prod[Vercel]
        P1[enqueueJob] --> P2[MongoDB Jobs] --> P3[Vercel Cron]
    end
    subgraph Azure[Azure]
        A1[enqueueJob] --> A2[Service Bus] --> A3[Container Apps]
    end
    D2 -.->|evolves to| P2
    P2 -.->|evolves to| A2
```

No redesign needed when moving from Vercel to Azure. Swap the queue adapter and worker target.

blocks.content: **Goal: cheap, simple, fast development.** No Redis, no BullMQ — just Next.js, MongoDB, and local dev.
This is the initial real production deployment. **Vercel** is used as the main application hosting platform — no servers, no Docker hosts, no load balancers to manage.

### Why this is attractive

- No server management
- No Docker host maintenance
- No OS updates
- No load balancer configuration
- No deployment infrastructure
- No scaling concerns for the Next.js application

Vercel handles the application layer. MongoDB, file storage, and analytics are independently scalable.

### Cost target: ≤ $80/month

| Item | Est. Cost |
|---|---|
| Vercel | ~$20 |
| MongoDB Atlas M10 | ~$50–60 |
| Object storage | ~$1–5 |
| Redis | $0 initially |
| **Total** | **~$71–85** |

Redis should not be introduced unless actually needed.

This is the enterprise-oriented deployment. Application hosting and background processing move into Azure. MongoDB can remain MongoDB Atlas unless Bahri specifically requires the database inside Azure.
The queue is the most important abstraction in the system. The application code calls the same interface regardless of environment — only the backing implementation changes.

No redesign needed when moving from Vercel to Azure. Swap the queue adapter and worker target.

### Code pattern

```text
Development:
enqueueJob() → MongoDB jobs → Local worker

Vercel:
enqueueJob() → MongoDB jobs → Vercel Cron / serverless

Azure:
enqueueJob() → Azure Service Bus → Container Apps Worker
```
BBS is architected as six independent layers. The application itself doesn't fundamentally change between environments — infrastructure evolves underneath.

### Redis is an optimization, not a foundation

Redis should not be a foundational dependency. The fundamental architecture is:

**Next.js → MongoDB → Object Storage → Queue → Worker**

Redis can be added later when monitoring proves caching is needed.

For the projected scale — **~2,000 MAU, ~20,000 submissions/month, ~150,000 records/year** — MongoDB alone is more than sufficient.

input.description: Technical architecture for the BBS project — development, Vercel production, and Azure enterprise deployment with six-layer design.

blocks.content: **Goal: cheap, simple, fast development.** No Redis, no BullMQ — just Next.js, MongoDB, and local dev.
This is the initial real production deployment. **Vercel** is used as the main application hosting platform — no servers, no Docker hosts, no load balancers to manage.

### Why this is attractive

- No server management
- No Docker host maintenance
- No OS updates
- No load balancer configuration
- No deployment infrastructure
- No scaling concerns for the Next.js application

Vercel handles the application layer. MongoDB, file storage, and analytics are independently scalable.

### Cost target: ≤ $80/month

| Item | Est. Cost |
|---|---|
| Vercel | ~$20 |
| MongoDB Atlas M10 | ~$50–60 |
| Object storage | ~$1–5 |
| Redis | $0 initially |
| **Total** | **~$71–85** |

Redis should not be introduced unless actually needed.

This is the enterprise-oriented deployment. Application hosting and background processing move into Azure. MongoDB can remain MongoDB Atlas unless Bahri specifically requires the database inside Azure.
The queue is the most important abstraction in the system. The application code calls the same interface regardless of environment — only the backing implementation changes.

No redesign needed when moving from Vercel to Azure. Swap the queue adapter and worker target.

### Code pattern

```text
Development:
enqueueJob() → MongoDB jobs → Local worker

Vercel:
enqueueJob() → MongoDB jobs → Vercel Cron / serverless

Azure:
enqueueJob() → Azure Service Bus → Container Apps Worker
```
BBS is architected as six independent layers. The application itself doesn't fundamentally change between environments — infrastructure evolves underneath.

### Redis is an optimization, not a foundation

Redis should not be a foundational dependency. The fundamental architecture is:

**Next.js → MongoDB → Object Storage → Queue → Worker**

Redis can be added later when monitoring proves caching is needed.

For the projected scale — **~2,000 MAU, ~20,000 submissions/month, ~150,000 records/year** — MongoDB alone is more than sufficient.

### Background jobs on Vercel

Vercel has no long-running processes, so background work runs via **Vercel Cron**:

- Cron hits a Next.js route on a schedule
- The route drains the MongoDB `jobs` collection
- Serverless functions do the work and mark jobs complete

### Why not servers

- No server management, no Docker hosts, no OS updates
- No load balancer configuration
- No deployment infrastructure
- Vercel scales the app layer automatically

MongoDB, file storage, and analytics scale independently of Vercel.

### When to move to Azure

Move when an enterprise customer (e.g. Bahri) requires:

- Data residency / database inside their Azure tenant
- Managed identity and Entra ID integration
- Long-running workers (not serverless)
- Guaranteed queue delivery via Service Bus
- Compliance and audit requirements

### What changes vs. what stays

| Concern | Change |
|---|---|
| App hosting | Vercel → Azure App Service |
| Workers | Vercel Cron → Azure Container Apps |
| Queue | MongoDB jobs → Azure Service Bus |
| Files | S3 → Azure Blob Storage |
| Database | MongoDB Atlas (unchanged, unless in-Azure required) |

The application code stays the same — only the queue adapter and worker target swap.

### Layer responsibilities

1. **Frontend** — Next.js + React + shadcn/ui. Server components for data-heavy pages, client components for interactivity.
2. **Application** — Route Handlers + business logic/services. Owns all domain rules; no infrastructure code leaks in.
3. **Authentication** — custom auth today, Entra ID in Azure. Abstracted so the provider can swap.
4. **Data Layer** — MongoDB Atlas. Operational collections for CRUD, analytics collections for reporting. Indexes tuned per query pattern.
5. **File Storage** — S3/CloudFront (or Azure Blob). Presigned URLs for upload/download; app never proxies large files.
6. **Asynchronous Layer** — the queue + worker. Everything slow (notifications, exports, scheduled jobs) goes through here.

### When Redis *would* be justified

Add Redis only if monitoring shows a real bottleneck, for example:

- Repeated expensive aggregations (dashboard/reporting)
- Hot read path on submissions needing sub-10ms latency
- Session/cache sharing across many serverless instances

### Scale sanity check

| Metric | Projected |
|---|---|
| Monthly active users | ~2,000 |
| Submissions / month | ~20,000 |
| Records / year | ~150,000 |

At this scale MongoDB's built-in indexes and aggregation pipeline handle everything comfortably. Premature Redis adds cost and operational surface for no measurable gain.
